question: A pipe just burst in my house. What do I do in the next few minutes, and will homeowners insurance pay for the damage?
verdictConfirmed: Regulators say most homeowners policies cover damage from a 'sudden and accidental' discharge from plumbing, with a condition: the home was kept heated (and, if vacant, the water shut off and drained). A burst pipe inside one house is not a 'flood' under the federal flood policy, which needs two or more acres or two or more properties. First steps: close the main valve, keep away from wet electrics, dry within 24-48 hours.

facts.claim: Charlotte Water (city utility) says the master shut-off valve is on the house side of the meter inside the house: near the front wall closest to the street in a basement or crawl space home, near the water heater or in the garage on a slab, typically where plumbing enters the building. Gate valves turn clockwise; ball valves turn perpendicular to the pipe.
facts.quote: If a water pipe bursts, it is important to know how to turn the water off before your home is flooded. Your master shut off valve is located on the house side of your meter inside the house. If you have a basement or crawl space, the main water shut-off is probably located in the basement, near the front wall of your home (closest to the street). If your home was built on a slab, the main water shut-off could be located near your hot water heater or inside of your garage. Master Shut-off valve for your drinking water is typically where plumbing enters a building. Once you find the shutoff valve you will either hand turn it (clockwise for gate valves and perpendicular to the pipe for ball valves).

facts.claim: Ready.gov (FEMA) flood guidance: do not touch wet electrical equipment or touch electrical equipment while standing in water; turn off electricity only if it is safe to do so. Page last updated 11/18/2026.
facts.quote: Do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Turn off the electricity to prevent electric shock if it is safe to do so.

facts.claim: DC Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking: most homeowner policies generally cover damage from a frozen pipe that bursts when the damage resulted from a 'sudden and accidental' discharge from a plumbing source; the policy may not respond if you neglected to safeguard the property; policies usually require heat to be maintained, some a certain temperature even if vacant; a vacant or unoccupied property with no heat should have the water supply shut off and the systems drained.
facts.quote: Most homeowner and commercial property insurance policies, in general, will cover damage from a frozen pipe that bursts. Coverage usually exists if the policy contains the following or similar language: Coverage is provided when it is determined damage resulted from a “sudden and accidental” discharge from a plumbing source or system ... your insurance policy may not respond if it appears you neglected to take the proper steps to safeguard your property. Your policy usually requires that heat be maintained within the property, and some policies require that you maintain a certain temperature, even if the property is vacant, occupied or unoccupied. ... If your vacant or unoccupied property has no heat, be sure to shut off the water supply and drain the system(s) and appliance(s) of water to avoid freezing pipes.

facts.claim: Massachusetts Division of Insurance, 1/21/2026: in 2024, 48.6% of homeowners' insurance claims in Massachusetts were for non-flood water losses and freezing-related damage.
facts.quote: According to our most recent home insurance report, in 2024, 48.6% of homeowners’ insurance claims in Massachusetts were for non‑flood water losses and freezing‑related damage.

facts.claim: NAIC consumer article (dateModified 2024-02-08): homeowners policies cover damage from a 'sudden and accidental' discharge from a plumbing system; policies generally require a minimum temperature; if the insurer determines you neglected your plumbing system, burst-pipe damage may not be covered.
facts.quote: Homeowners policies cover damage from a “sudden and accidental” discharge from a plumbing system. ... Policies generally require homeowners to maintain the home at a minimum temperature ... If your insurance company determines you neglected your plumbing system ... the damage from a burst pipe may not be covered.

facts.claim: The federal Standard Flood Insurance Policy (Dwelling Form, 44 CFR Part 61, Appendix A(1)) defines flood as a general and temporary condition of inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land or of two or more properties (one of which is yours), from overflow of inland or tidal waters, unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters, or mudflow. A pipe bursting inside one house does not meet that definition.
facts.quote: Flood, as used in this flood insurance policy, means: 1. A general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (one of which is your property) from: a. Overflow of inland or tidal waters; b. Unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source; c. Mudflow.

facts.claim: EPA (page last updated February 18, 2026): dry water-damaged areas and items within 24-48 hours to prevent mold growth; mold may be hidden behind drywall, under carpets and pads.
facts.quote: It is important to dry water-damaged areas and items within 24-48 hours to prevent mold growth. ... If wet or damp materials or areas are dried 24-48 hours after a leak or spill happens, in most cases mold will not grow. ... Mold may be hidden in places such as the back side of dry wall, wallpaper, or paneling, the top side of ceiling tiles, the underside of carpets and pads
